title: The Happiest People Aren't Passionate About Everything
essay_markdown:
Here's a finding that might change how you look at your to-do list: according to PsyPost's report on a study in *Motivation and Emotion*, led by Robert Vallerand, a professor at the University of Quebec at Montreal, the happiest people are not simply passionate about everything. They apply their passion selectively, pouring it into activities they truly enjoy.

Read that again, because it's freeing. Happiness isn't about manufacturing enthusiasm for every task on your plate. The study found that harmonious passion for enjoyable activities positively predicted positive emotions, and those positive emotions were in turn associated with higher psychological well-being. Choose the right things to love, and the good feelings follow.

The same study adds a wrinkle worth respecting: the happiest people still approach less enjoyable tasks, like chores, with a sense of autonomy and self-motivation. They don't abandon the dishes. They own them. They decide to do them rather than feeling dragged.

Now, what does it look like when someone takes this seriously at full scale? Ashley J. Hobbs, 32, of Washington, D.C., offers one answer. As she told Essence, she left her job after about a year and a half in a marketing communication role for local government. She had begun to think intentionally about what success and happiness looked like for her, and she realized she was doing a disservice to her dreams by keeping up a happy face. Her reasoning was simple and brave: "Although I was nervous, I decided to just bet on myself." Looking back, she wrote that quitting was absolutely worth it, citing the peace and clarity she was gaining about her purpose. Her side business, three years of photography, was already waiting for more of her attention.

Notice what she didn't do. She didn't wait until she felt fearless. She was nervous and moved anyway.

Which brings us to today's idea: do the things you love, because life is too precious to be doing anything else. If you don't enjoy something, don't do it. Spend your time and energy on what brings you fulfillment and happiness.

You don't have to resign from anything to live this. Hobbs's story is the dramatic end of a spectrum, and most of your wins will come at the small end. The research suggests the aim isn't to eliminate everything unpleasant. It's to stop pouring your best energy into things that give nothing back, and to be deliberate about the things that do.

So here's how to use this today.

First, find one thing you're doing out of pure habit or obligation that you truly don't enjoy, and that nobody is actually depending on you for. A standing meeting you attend by default. A commitment you said yes to out of politeness. A hobby you keep up because you once told people you did it. Drop it, or at least start the conversation about dropping it.

Second, give that reclaimed time to something that lights you up, even for twenty minutes. Pick up the camera, the guitar, the sketchbook, the running shoes. Don't wait for a free weekend.

Third, for the tasks you can't escape, borrow the happiest people's trick: choose them. Say, "I'm doing this because I want a clean kitchen to wake up to," and notice how the weight shifts.

This is not selfishness. It's stewardship of the one limited resource you can't earn back. Every hour spent on something you love is an hour well spent, and every hour you reclaim from something hollow is a gift to your future self.

So go be selective today. Don't try to be passionate about everything. Be passionate about the right things, and meet the rest with a steady, self-chosen shrug. That's what the happiest people do.
